newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Sikhs want Queen to visit Amritsar shrine.
newsitem.headline: India's Sikhs want Queen to visit Amritsar shrine.

text.p: Sikh groups protested on Monday at the Indian government's apparent attempt to head off a trip by Queen Elizabeth to their holiest shrine, and Britain said details for the visit were still being finalised.

Indian Prime Minister Inder Kujmar Gujral said in an interview published on Sunday he wanted the British monarch to stay away from the city of Amritsar to avoid stirring up bitterness over the 1919 Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
"We are still discussing the details of the Queen's programme (with New Delhi)," a Foreign Office spokesman said in London.
British troops killed 379 unarmed demonstrators herded into a square in Amritsar on April 13, 1919, in one of the most notorious incidents in the history of the British empire.

Gurcharan Singh Tohra, head of the organisation that administers India's Sikh shrines, said "vested interests" were trying to prevent the queen from paying her respects at the Sikh religion's holiest shrine, Amritsar's Golden Temple.
The Press Trust of India quoted Tohra as saying the queen would be given a "most profuse and warm welcome".
"No condition should be imposed on persons coming to the temple to pay obeisance," Tohra said.

Simranjit Singh Mann, who leads a breakaway faction of the Akali Dal, the Sikhs' main political party, said in a statement Gujral was trying to "scuttle" the international focus the queen's visit would give to Amritsar and the Sikhs.
"Irrespective of the occasion of the visit, it is not mandatory for any individual who is visiting Amritsar to include the Jallianwala Bagh on his/her itinerary," Mann said.
India's foreign ministry said in a statement: "The programme for the visit of the Queen has been under discussion with the British side for several weeks. The visit constitutes an important event.

"In order to ensure that this important relationship with a very friendly country is insulated from controversy, (the Indian) government have drawn the attention of the British government to the sentiments being expressed on the proposed visit to Amritsar."

The queen is due to start a visit to India around October 12. Earlier this month the British High Commission in New Delhi would only confirm that a reconnaissance team had visited Amritsar but added that no final decision had been taken on a visit.
Some Indian commentators have said the queen ought to use her visit to apologise for the massacre, but others say the visit alone would be an act of atonement.
Gujral told the British newspaper the Observer on Sunday: "It is a goodwill visit and we would not like to add anything historically that would cause bitterness."
"We have suggested as a government to the British a few days back that it would be much better if she doesn't visit Amritsar."
British officials, however, said Gujral's remarks did not accord completely with what London had previously understood to be Delhi's position. Britain was therefore seeking clarification.
The Queen had been due to go to Amritsar to visit the Sikh Golden Temple as part of a tour marking the 50th anniversary of the end of British imperial rule in the subcontinent.
